summary: Describes test cases for evaluating congestion control algorithms for interactive real-time RTP media in a controlled environment. It is informational and works with the evaluation guidelines in RFC 8868.

plainLanguage.summary: Before letting a new video-call traffic rule loose on the real Internet, you try it on a practice track. This document lists the practice courses to test it on.

subtitle: Standardized test scenarios for evaluating congestion control in real-time media

tldr.problem: Before deploying new congestion control algorithms for interactive real-time media like video calls, developers need a standard way to test them in controlled environments that match real-world conditions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8867 defines test cases covering various network scenarios—changing capacity, competing flows, wireless challenges—with precise topology definitions, evaluation metrics, and expected behaviors so algorithms can be compared consistently.
tldr.outcome: These test cases became the foundation for evaluating RTP-based congestion control algorithms, complementing RFC 8868's evaluation guidelines with specific, repeatable scenarios.

today: RFC 8867 is an Informational document published in January 2021 and remains the standard reference for evaluating congestion control algorithms in real-time interactive media. It is used by implementers developing and testing new algorithms before deployment and by researchers evaluating protocol enhancements.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) is widely used for multimedia communication like video conferences. For RTP applications to work well, they need to implement congestion control—algorithms that adapt the sending rate when the network gets congested, similar to how TCP adapts on the Internet. RFC 8867 provides a structured set of test cases for evaluating how well these congestion control algorithms work in controlled lab environments.

The test cases are based on RFC 8868's evaluation guidelines and RFC 8836's requirements. They cover basic scenarios that occur in real networks, using a common structure that makes it easy to add new tests as needed. The key insight is that every candidate algorithm should be tested against the same scenarios so they can be compared fairly.
sections.plainLanguage: Video calls need to be smart about how fast they send data. When the Internet gets crowded, they need to slow down. This document gives a recipe for testing whether a new smart algorithm really works before putting it into millions of phones.

sections.title: Test Case Structure and Setup
sections.content:
Each test case follows a consistent structure to make implementation easier. A test defines its general description and motivation, the expected behavior of the algorithm under test, the metrics needed to evaluate performance, and the testbed topology showing how sources and receivers connect.

The testbed attributes describe the test duration, path characteristics (bottleneck capacity, propagation delay, jitter, queue type, and loss ratio), and application-related settings like media types, codec details, and competing traffic. The reference bottleneck capacity is 1 Mbps, one-way propagation delay is 50 ms, and jitter is up to 30 ms, with a tail-drop queue of 300 ms unless the test specifies otherwise. Media sources typically use Variable Bit Rate (VBR) video ranging from 150 Kbps to 1.5 Mbps and Constant Bit Rate (CBR) audio at 20 Kbps.
sections.plainLanguage: Every test follows the same checklist: what we're testing for, how the network is set up, which numbers to measure, and how the algorithm should behave. This way, when you test a new algorithm, you can use the same checklist and compare results fairly.

sections.title: Core Test Scenarios
sections.content:
RFC 8867 defines eight basic test scenarios covering the most important situations a congestion control algorithm will face. The first two test single and multiple media flows facing variable available capacity—checking if the algorithm detects and adapts to changing bottleneck bandwidth without oscillating wildly. The third test puts both media and feedback traffic on the same congested link to simulate asymmetric networks. The fourth tests multiple flows using the same algorithm competing for the same capacity.

Test 5 evaluates fairness between flows with different round-trip times (RTTs)—a key property since slow paths should not starve fast paths. Tests 6 and 7 measure how the algorithm competes with long-lived TCP flows (like large file downloads) and short-lived TCP flows respectively. Test 8 measures how the algorithm behaves when media pauses and resumes, which happens in real calls when someone mutes or stops video.
sections.plainLanguage: The tests cover common real-life situations: when the network gets faster or slower, when multiple video calls happen at once, when the Internet is already busy with other traffic, when video pauses, and when people in different parts of the world (with different delays) are on the same call.

sections.title: Evaluation Metrics and Performance Measurement
sections.content:
To evaluate an algorithm's performance, developers must measure specific metrics at fine time granularity. Flow-level metrics include end-to-end delay (how long a packet takes to reach the receiver), variations in sending bit rate and throughput (watching for unwanted oscillations), packet losses at the receiver, feedback message overhead, and convergence time (how long it takes to reach steady state). Transport-level metrics are bandwidth utilization (how much of the available capacity is used) and queue length in milliseconds.

Measurements are typically taken in 200 ms time windows to capture the behavior of the algorithm as it adapts. The RFC recommends logging enough detail to visualize these metrics so different algorithms can be compared graphically. This empirical approach lets engineers see whether an algorithm is smooth (low oscillation), fair (all flows get equal capacity), responsive (adapts quickly to changes), and efficient (uses most of the available bandwidth).
sections.plainLanguage: Engineers watch numbers like how long packets take to arrive, how smoothly the video bitrate changes, whether packets get lost, and how quickly the algorithm figures out the right speed for the network. A good algorithm is smooth, fair to other flows, quick to adapt, and doesn't waste bandwidth.

sections.title: Additional Scenarios and Considerations
sections.content:
Beyond the eight basic test cases, RFC 8867 suggests several other important scenarios. Media flows with priority allow testing whether an algorithm can handle differentiated quality-of-service requirements. Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) usage tests whether the algorithm can make use of network feedback beyond simple packet loss. Multiple bottlenecks test the algorithm when the path has congestion at multiple points rather than just one chokepoint.

RFC 8869 extends these tests to wireless networks (both cellular and Wi-Fi), where path capacity and delay can change rapidly and unpredictably. The document also references RFC 8868, which provides the broader evaluation guidelines and additional considerations for designing rigorous tests. Implementers are encouraged to expand the test suite for their specific use cases while maintaining the common structure so results remain comparable.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks are more complicated: they might give priority to certain traffic, they might send special signals about congestion, or the congestion might happen in multiple places at once. The document gives examples of these trickier situations too, and notes that wireless networks need even more special tests because phone and Wi-Fi speeds change so much faster.
